Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 57, verse 3 (part 1 of 2):

(A wonderful benefit)
The rule is that a thing is not conjoined (ʿaṭf) to itself, because the particles of conjunction (ḥurūf al-ʿaṭf) function as the repetition of the governing verb. For when you say qāma Zaydun wa-ʿAmrun ("Zayd stood and ʿAmr"), it means qāma Zaydun wa-qāma ʿAmrun ("Zayd stood, and ʿAmr stood"), and the second is other than the first. So when you find something like their saying kadhiban wa-mīnan ("a liar and a sinner"), it indicates an additional meaning in the second word, even if it is hidden from you. For this reason it is very unlikely that one would say in their speech: jāʾanī ʿUmar wa-Abū Ḥafṣ ("ʿUmar and Abū Ḥafṣ came to me"), or: raḍiya Allāhu ʿan Abī Bakrin wa-ʿatīqihi ("may Allah be pleased with Abū Bakr and his ʿatīq"), since the wāw (conjunction) only joins two things, not one thing with itself. When the second name carries a meaning beyond the meaning of the first name, you have the choice of conjoining or not. If you conjoin, it is because you intend to enumerate attributes, which are distinct. If you do not conjoin, it is because each of them carries a pronoun referring to the first. In the first case you say: Zaydun faqīhun shāʿirun kātibun ("Zayd is a jurist, poet, writer"), and in the second: Zaydun faqīhun wa-shāʿirun wa-kātibun, as if you had conjoined writing to poetry with the wāw. Where you do not conjoin, you have made the second follow the first, because it is the same from the standpoint that the bearer of the attributes is one.

As for the names of the Lord, Blessed and Exalted, most of them come in the Qur'an without conjunction, such as al-Samīʿ al-ʿAlīm, al-ʿAzīz al-Ḥakīm, al-Ghafūr al-Raḥīm, (al-Malik al-Quddūs al-Salām), and so on to the end.

They come conjoined in two places. One is in four names, which are (al-Awwal, al-Ākhir, al-Ẓāhir, al-Bāṭin). The other is in some attributes with the relative pronoun, such as His saying: ﴿Who created and proportioned, and who determined and guided, and who brought forth the pasture﴾.
Its parallel: ﴿Who made for you the earth as a cradle and made for you therein roads that you may be guided, and who sent down from the sky water in measure, and We revived thereby a dead land; thus you will be brought forth, and who created all the pairs﴾.
As for omitting the conjunction in general, it is because of the affinity between the meanings of those names and the nearness of some of them to others, and because the mind's awareness of the second is like its awareness of the first.
Do you not see that when you become aware of the attribute of forgiveness, your mind passes from it to mercy? Likewise, when you become aware of the attribute of hearing, the mind passes to sight.
Likewise: ﴿al-Khāliq, al-Bārīʾ, al-Muṣawwir﴾.
As for those four names, they are words of differing meanings and opposing realities in their original application, but they are of agreeing meanings and corresponding in respect of the Lord, exalted is He; no meaning of them is left apart from Him. Rather, He is (the First) just as He is (the Last), and (the Outward) just as He is (the Inward), and they do not contradict one another in regard to Him.
So the entry of the wāw served to turn away the listener's assumption, before reflection and consideration, of the notion of the impossible and the possibility of opposites, because a thing cannot be outward and inward from one aspect; rather that is by two considerations.
So conjunction here is better than omitting it for this wisdom.
This is the answer of al-Suhaylī.
And better than it to say: since these words indicate differing meanings, and perfection in being described by them despite their differences, He brought the particle of conjunction which signifies difference between the conjoined terms, as a notification that these meanings, despite their differences, are established for the one described by them.
Another aspect, better than these, is that the wāw requires the affirmation of the preceding description, and its confirmation is, within the speech, containing a kind of additional emphasis of reinforcement.
An illustration of that, a stepping stone to understanding what we are about, is:
If a man, for example, has four attributes: he is knowledgeable, generous, brave, and wealthy, and the listener does not know that or does not acknowledge it, and wonders at the combination of these attributes in one man,
then when you say: "Zayd is knowledgeable," and his mind seems to find it unlikely, you say: "and generous," that is, "and along with that he is generous," then: "and brave," that is, "and along with that he is brave," and "and wealthy." So in the conjunction there is an extra confirmation and emphasis not obtained without it,
by which you ward off the assumption of denial.
Knowing this, the notion may be prone to denying that these opposites are combined in one described subject.
So when it is said: "He is the First," the assumption may spread that being first requires that the Last be other than Him, since firstness and lastness are correlatives. Likewise the Outward and the Inward: when it is said "He is the Outward," the assumption may spread that the Inward is its opposite. So this assumption is cut off by the particle of conjunction, which signifies that the One described as First is the One described as Last, as if it were said: "He is the First, and He is the Last, and He is the Outward, and He is the Inward, and none other."
Reflect on this, for it is among the subtleties and fine points of the Arabic language.
What clarifies this for you is that if a town, for example, has a judge, a preacher, and an emir, and they are all combined in one man, it is good to say: "Zayd is the preacher, the judge, and the emir."
Here the conjunction has a merit that the bare epithet lacks, so conjoining the attributes here is better beyond doubt, to cut off the assumption of one who supposes that the preacher is other than the emir and the emir other than the judge.

(Another benefit)
"He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, guided whoever is afflicted with something of the whispering of infinite regress concerning agents, when it is said to him: 'This is Allah who created creation; then who created Allah?', to recite: ﴿He is the First and the Last and the Outward and the Inward, and He is, of all things, Knowing﴾ [al-Ḥadīd: 3]."
Likewise, "Ibn ʿAbbās said to Abū Zumayl Simāk ibn al-Walīd al-Ḥanafī, when he asked him: 'What is the thing I find in my chest?' He said: 'What is it?' He said: 'I said: By Allah, I will not speak of it.' He said to me: 'Is it something of doubt?' I said: 'Yes.' He said to me: 'None escapes that. Until Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿So if you are in doubt concerning what We have sent down to you, then ask those who read the Scripture before you﴾ [Yūnus: 94].'
He said: 'Then he said to me: When you find something in yourself, say: ﴿He is the First and the Last and the Outward and the Inward, and He is, of all things, Knowing﴾.'"
Thus he guided them with this verse to the invalidity of the vain infinite regress by the self-evident judgment of reason, and that the chain of created things in its beginning ends at a First before which there is nothing, just as in its end it ends at a Last after which there is nothing. Likewise His outwardness is the loftiness above which there is nothing, and His inwardness is the encompassing in which there is nothing beneath Him. For if there were something before Him that influenced Him, that would be the Lord, the Creator; and the matter must end at an uncreated Creator who is self-sufficient and independent of anything else. Everything is in need of Him, self-subsisting, and everything subsisting by Him is existent in its own essence, and everything exists by Him. He is eternal without a beginning. Everything other than Him, its existence after its non-existence, subsists by its own essence, and the subsistence of everything is by Him. He is thus the First before whom there is nothing, the Last after whom there is nothing, the Outward above whom there is nothing, the Inward beneath whom there is nothing.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "People will not cease asking questions until one of them says: 'This is Allah who created creation; then who created Allah?' Whoever finds anything of that, let him seek refuge in Allah and desist."
And Allah, the Exalted, has said: ﴿And if an evil prompting from Satan should tempt you, then seek refuge in Allah; indeed, He is the Hearing, the Knowing﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 36].

(Section)
The point is that worship through His name (al-Ẓāhir) gathers the heart upon the one worshipped, and makes for it a Lord to aim at, a Ṣamad to turn to in its needs, and a refuge to take shelter in. When that settles in the heart and one knows one's Lord by His name al-Ẓāhir, one's servanthood is made upright, and He becomes for one a stronghold and a resort, to which one takes refuge, flees, and runs at every time. As for worship through His name al-Bāṭin, it is a matter whose expression is constricted in describing its reality, the tongue is weary of describing it, allusion is confounded by it, and expression falls short of it. For it requires a knowledge free from the impurities of negation (taʿṭīl), purified from the dung of anthropomorphism (tashbīh), exempt from the filth of incarnation (ḥulūl) and unity with creation (ittiḥād), and an expression conveying the meaning and disclosing it, and a sound taste untainted by the tastes of those who deviate. Whoever is granted this understands the meaning of His name al-Bāṭin, and worship through it is sound for him. Glory be to Allah, how many feet have slipped in this station, and how many understandings have strayed in it! The heretic composed in it with the tongue of the sincere, so that the brethren of the Christians were confused with the sincere monotheists, because understandings fall short of it and it is hard to separate truth from falsehood in it, and what is in the mind is confused with what is outside, except for one whom Allah has granted insight into the truth, and a light by which he distinguishes guidance from error, and a criterion by which he differentiates truth from falsehood, and who has, besides that, knowledge of the causes of error, the divergence of paths, and the sources of mistake. Thus he has insight into truth and falsehood. That is the bounty of Allah, which He gives to whom He wills, and Allah is the Possessor of great bounty.

The gateway to this knowledge and worship is knowing the encompassing of the Lord [Blessed and Exalted] over the world and His greatness, and that all worlds are in His grasp, and that the seven heavens and the seven earths are in His hand like a mustard seed in the hand of a servant. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And when We said to you: Indeed your Lord encompasses the people﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 60], and He said: ﴿And Allah, from behind them, is encompassing﴾ [al-Burūj: 20]. For this reason He, glory be to Him, pairs these two names which indicate these two meanings: the name of Highness, which indicates that He is (al-Ẓāhir) and that nothing is above Him, and the name of Greatness, which indicates encompassing and that nothing is beneath Him, as He said: ﴿And He is the Most High, the Mighty﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255], and He said: ﴿And He is the Most High, the Great﴾ [Sabaʾ: 23], and He said: ﴿And to Allah belong the east and the west; so wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah. Indeed, Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 115].
He, Blessed and Exalted, as He is High over His creation in His essence, so nothing is above Him, is also the Inward in His essence, so nothing is beneath Him. Rather, He manifested over every thing, so He was above it, and He was inward, so He was nearer to every thing than itself. He encompasses it, whereas a thing does not encompass itself; and every thing is in His grasp, while nothing is in the grasp of itself. This is nearer to the general encompassing.

As for the nearness mentioned in the Qur'an and the Sunnah, it is the special nearness to His worshippers, supplicants and callers, and it is a fruit of worship through His name al-Bāṭin. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And when My servants ask you about Me, indeed I am near; I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾ [al-Baqarah: 186].
That is His nearness to the one who calls upon Him. And He said: ﴿Indeed, the mercy of Allah is near to the doers of good﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 56].
Here the predicate "near" (qarīb) came in the masculine form, though the subject "mercy" (raḥma) is feminine, as a notification of His nearness to the good-doers; as if He said: indeed Allah, by His mercy, is near to the good-doers. In the Ṣaḥīḥ, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, it is related that he said: "The closest a servant is to his Lord is when he is prostrating," and "The closest the Lord is to His servant is in the last part of the night." This is a special nearness, other than the nearness of encompassing and the nearness of inwardness.
In the Ṣaḥīḥ, from the hadith of Abū Mūsā: they were with the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, on a journey, and their voices rose with takbīr, so he said: "O people, be gentle with yourselves, for you are not calling upon one who is deaf or absent. Indeed the One you are calling upon is Hearing and Near, nearer to one of you than the neck of his mount." This is His nearness to the one who calls upon Him and remembers Him. That is, what need have you to raise your voices, when by His nearness He hears them whether lowered or raised, as He hears them when raised; for He is Hearing and Near. This nearness is among the requirements of love: the greater the love, the greater the nearness. The love of the Beloved takes hold of the heart of the lover, so that he passes away from all else by it, and his beloved overcomes his heart until it is as if he sees and witnesses Him.
If he does not have correct knowledge of Allah and of what is due to Him and what is impossible for Him, it leads him to the door of incarnation, if he does not enter it. Its cause is weakness of discrimination and the strength of the authority of love, and the Beloved's taking possession of his heart so that he is absent from observing anything else. In such a state he says: "Glory be to me," or "There is nothing in the robe but Allah," and similar ecstatic utterances (shaṭaḥāt), whose end is that he is forgiven and excused for his intoxication and his lack of discrimination in that state. So worship through this name is worship through pure love and the clarity of affection, and that the God be nearer to him than everything and nearer to him than himself, while being Outward, with nothing above Him. Whoever's intellect is dull and whose nature is coarse from grasping this, let him turn away from it gently toward what is more fitting for him, for it has been said:
"If you are not able to do something, leave it, and pass beyond it to what you are able to do."
Whoever has no taste for the nearness of love, and no knowledge of the nearness of the Beloved, the nearness of ultimate closeness, even if between them is the utmost distance (and especially when love is from both sides, a love free from defects, impurities, and corrupting accidents), the lover often finds his beloved overcoming his heart and his remembrance, he passes away from others, his heart softens and his soul is stripped bare, so he witnesses his beloved as present with him, close to him, though between them is the distance that separates them. In this state his mental existence is in his heart and his verbal existence is on his tongue, and this witnessing overpowers him and absorbs him, so he thinks that the external existence is in his sight by the predominance of the heart and spirit's rule, as it has been said:
"Your phantom is in my eye, your remembrance in my mouth, and your abode in my heart; so where can you be absent?"
Moreover, that Beloved is himself between him and his enemy at a distance, even if the bodies draw near and the dwellings are adjacent. The point is that the mental image is other than the external reality, though it corresponds to it; but the mental image has its locus in the heart and the external reality has its locus outside. Knowledge of these four names, namely the First, the Last, the Outward, and the Inward, constitutes the pillars of knowledge and gnosis, so it is fitting for the servant to reach in knowing them as far as his capacities and understanding can reach.

Know that you yourself have a first, a last, an outward and an inward; indeed every thing has a first, a last, an outward and an inward, even the passing thought, the moment, the breath, and less or more than that. The firstness of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, precedes the firstness of every other thing, and His lastness is established after the lastness of every other thing. So His firstness is His preceding of every thing, His lastness is His subsistence after every thing, His outwardness, exalted is He, is His highness and loftiness over every thing (outwardness entails loftiness, and the outward of a thing is what is high of it and encompasses its inward), and His inwardness, exalted is He, is His encompassing of every thing such that He is nearer to it than itself. This nearness is other than the nearness of the lover to his beloved; this is one kind and that is another. The matter of these four names rests on encompassing, and it is of two kinds, temporal and spatial. His firstness and lastness encompass by priority and posteriority: every prior thing ends at His firstness, and every later thing ends at His lastness. His outwardness and inwardness encompass every outward and inward: there is no outward but Allah is above it, no inward but Allah is beneath it, no first but Allah is before it, and no last but Allah is after it. So the First is His preexistence, the Last is His permanence and subsistence, the Outward is His loftiness and greatness, and the Inward is His nearness and closeness. He precedes every thing by His firstness, subsists after every thing by His lastness, is high over every thing by His outwardness, and is near to every thing by His inwardness. Thus no heaven conceals Him from heaven, nor earth earth; the outward is not veiled from Him by the inward, but rather the inward is outward to Him; the unseen is witnessed by Him, the far is near to Him, and the secret is public to Him. These four names comprise the pillars of tawḥīd. He is the First in His lastness and the Last in His firstness, the Outward in His inwardness and the Inward in His outwardness; He has never ceased to be First, Last, Outward and Inward.

The worship through these names has two ranks. The first rank is that you witness His priority (al-awwaliyya) in everything, His posteriority (al-akhiriyya) after everything, His exaltedness and His being above everything, and His nearness and closeness beneath everything. The created being is veiled by its like from what is beneath it, so it becomes a barrier between itself and what is veiled. But the Lord, may His majesty be exalted, has nothing beneath Him that is nearer to creation than He is. The second rank of worship is that you deal with each name according to what it requires. So you treat His precedence, through His priority over everything, and His precedence through His grace and kindness over all causes, with what that requires of singling Him out, not turning to anything else, trusting none but Him, and relying on none other than Him. Who interceded for you in eternity, when you were not a thing worth mentioning, until He named you with the name of Islam, marked you with the mark of faith, made you among the people of the right hand, and granted you in that unseen realm the status of the believers? He preserved you from worshipping servants, and freed you from submitting to slavery to one who has a likeness or a rival. Then He turned the direction of your heart toward Him, may He be blessed and exalted, rather than anything else. So entreat the One who preserved you from prostrating to an idol, and who decreed for you a sure footing of truthfulness in the eternal decree, that He complete upon you a blessing which He began, whose priority came from Him without any cause from you. Turn your aspiration away from observing choice, do not incline to outward traces and effects, do not be content with the base and the lowly, and hold fast to lofty aims and exalted ranks, which are attained only through obedience to God.

Indeed, Almighty and Majestic God has decreed that what is with Him is not attained except through obeying Him. Whoever is for God as He wills, God is for him beyond what he wills. Whoever comes to Him, He receives from afar, and whoever acts by His power and strength, He softens iron for him. Whoever leaves something for His sake, He gives him more than he could ask. And whoever wills His religious purpose, wills what He wills. Then let your secret inner self be directed to the goal, and confine your love and drawing near to the One whose grace and kindness precede every cause from you. Indeed, He is the One who bestowed the causes upon you, prepared them for you, averted their obstacles from you, and brought you by them to your praiseworthy end.

So rely on Him alone, serve Him alone, and prefer His pleasure alone. Make His love and His good pleasure the Ka'ba of your heart, around which you never cease to circumambulate, touching its corners and standing at its threshold. O your success and your happiness, if He, glory be to Him, perceives this in your heart, what robes of His blessings and garments of His bounties will be poured upon you: "O Allah, there is none who can withhold what You have given, and none who can give what You have withheld, and the might of the mighty avails them nothing against You; glory be to You and praise be to You." Then worship Him by His other name, by making Him alone your ultimate goal, with no goal for you beyond Him and no object of seeking behind Him. Just as all last things end at Him, and He is after every last, so make your end toward Him, for "to your Lord is the final destination" (﴿وَأَنَّ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ الْمُنتَهَىٰ﴾). All causes and ultimate ends terminate in Him, so there is no target beyond Him that one can reach. This has already been alerted to, along with worshipping Him by His name the Outward (al-Zahir). As for worshipping Him by His name the Inward (al-Batin), when you witness His encompassing of the worlds, the nearness of the servants to Him, the manifestness of inner realities to Him, the disclosure of secrets to Him, and that there is nothing between Him and them, then deal with Him according to the requirement of this witnessing. Purify your inner secret for Him, for it is open before Him; set right your unseen for Him, for it is witnessed before Him; and purify your inner self for Him, for it is apparent to Him.

Consider how these four names are the sum of knowledge of God and the sum of servitude to Him. Here the servant's witnessing halts at the bounty of his Creator and His favor, so he sees nothing belonging to anyone else except through Him and His power and strength. He becomes absent, through the bounty of his True Master, from everything that comes from himself, whether something he leaned upon, adorned himself with, held as a treasure, kept for the day of his need, or relied upon for some important matter. All of that stems from the deficiency of his vision and its turning away from realities and roots toward causes and branches, as is the nature of natural inclination, desire, and the requirement of injustice and ignorance. "Indeed, man is wrongdoing and ignorant" (﴿إِنَّهُ كَانَ ظَلُومًا جَهُولًا﴾). Whoever God, glory be to Him, has polished of the rust of his insight, perfected his innate nature, and made him aware of the beginnings of affairs, their ends, their points of reference, their sources and their destinations, becomes, in truth, a bankrupt of his knowledge, deeds, states and tastes, saying: "I seek God's forgiveness for my knowledge and my deeds," meaning, for my attribution of them to myself and my absorption in them, away from the grace of Him who reminded me of them and began bestowing them upon me without any prior cause from me that would necessitate it. He witnesses nothing but the grace of his Master, the precedence of His favor, and its permanence. So his Master rewards him for this lofty witnessing with the reality of the middle poverty, between the lower and the higher poverty, with two rewards:

The first is deliverance from seeing his deeds, whereby he used to see them, praise himself by them, and regard them as abundant; so he becomes absorbed in contemplating grace, absent from them, passing away from them, annihilated from seeing them. The second reward is that He cuts him off from witnessing states, that is, from witnessing himself as multiplied by them. For the state has its seat in the breast, and the breast is the house of the heart and the self. When the gift descends into the breast to the heart, and the self stands firm to take its share of the gift, it praises itself by it, takes pride in it, exults, exalts itself, and establishes its selfhood, because it is ignorant and wrongdoing; and this is the requirement of ignorance and injustice.

When the light of the attribute of bestowal reaches the heart, and he witnesses the meaning of His name al-Mannan (the Bestower of favor), and God, glory be to Him, manifests Himself to the heart of His servant through this name together with His first name, the heart and self are stunned by it, and the servant becomes poor toward his Master by contemplating the precedence of His first grace. Thus he is cut off from witnessing any matter or state that he would attribute to himself, such that by his witnessing of his state he is severed and cut off from seeing the might of his Master and Originator and from observing His attributes.

So the one who witnesses states is cut off from seeing the favor and grace of his Creator and from contemplating the precedence of priority over all causes, and is absent, through witnessing the might of his own self, from the might of his Master. This matter is reversed for this poor servant: the vision of his Master's might and bounty and the contemplation of His precedence occupy him from any state by which the servant might take pride or be honored.

Likewise, returning to precedence through contemplating grace purifies one from the filth of contemplating stations. A station is what one is firmly established in, and a state is what passes and does not last. The contemplation of stations, the pride one takes in them, and his seeing himself as the possessor of a station he has realized and perfected, so that he deserves to be attributed to it and described by it, such as being called ascetic, patient, fearful, hopeful, loving, or content, his seeing himself as deserving that stations be ascribed to him and that he be described by them in the manner of entitlement, is a departure from poverty toward self-sufficiency, a leap to the stage of servitude, and ignorance of the right of lordship. Returning to precedence through contemplating grace absorbs the servant's aspiration and purifies him of such filth, so that he becomes clarified by the light of God, Almighty and Majestic, from the vile defects of these impurities.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 57, verse 13:

It has been said that the meaning is: "Return to the world and take from faith a light by which you may pass, as the believers did."

It has also been said: "Return behind you, to the place where the lights were distributed, and seek there a light by which you may pass."

Then a wall was set between them and the people of faith, with a gate. Its inner side, facing the believers, ﴿contains mercy﴾, and its outer side, facing them, ﴿from its outer side is punishment﴾.

When the believers cross the Sirat (the bridge), which none crosses except a believer, they are secure from entering the Fire. They are then detained at a bridge-like span (qantarah) between Paradise and the Fire, where retribution is taken for the wrongs they committed against one another in the world. When they have been purified, they are permitted to enter Paradise.

When the people of Paradise are settled in Paradise and the people of the Fire in the Fire, Death is brought in the form of a horned ram, white with black spots. It is stopped between Paradise and the Fire, and it is said: "O people of Paradise!" They look up, fearful. Then it is said: "O people of the Fire!" They look up, joyful. It is said: "Do you recognize this?" They say: "Yes," and all of them have recognized it. It is said: "This is Death." It is slaughtered between Paradise and the Fire. Then it is said: "O people of Paradise, eternity without death! O people of the Fire, eternity without death!"

This is the final state of this drop of semen, which is the origin of the human being. Between this origin and this end lie states and levels, decreed by the All-Mighty, the All-Knowing, which move the human being through them, level after level, until he reaches his final end of happiness or wretchedness.

﴿Destroyed is man; how disbelieving is he!﴾

(Admonition)

How will they be when they are gathered to the bridge of Hell (Jisr Jahannam)? It is thinner than a hair and sharper than a sword. It is slippery and dangerous, and it is dark. No one crosses it except with a light by which he can see where to place his feet. The lights are distributed among the people, according to their differing degrees of passage and progress. They are given an outward light along with the people of Islam, just as they were together in this world, performing prayer, zakat, pilgrimage, and fasting. When they reach the middle of the bridge, winds of hypocrisy blow upon their lights and extinguish the lamps in their hands. They stop, bewildered, unable to proceed. A wall is then set between them and the people of faith, with a gate. But the people are cut off from the keys. Its inner side, facing the believers, contains mercy, and what faces them from their side is punishment and vengeance. They call out to those who have gone ahead of them, the company of believers, whose torches shine from afar like stars, visible to the human eye: ﴿Wait for us, that we may borrow from your light.﴾

So that we may be able to pass through this narrow place, for our lights have gone out, and today there is no passage except with a lamp of light. ﴿It will be said: "Return behind you and seek light."﴾

That is where the lights were distributed. How remote is standing still for anyone in such a race!

How can we seek a place to stand in this narrow path?

Will anyone today turn back for anyone on this road?

Will any companion today turn toward a companion? So they remind them of their gathering with them and their companionship in this world, as a stranger reminds the homeland's native of their companionship on journeys. ﴿Were we not with you?﴾ We fasted as you fasted, prayed as you prayed, recited as you recited, gave charity as you gave charity, and performed pilgrimage as you performed it. What, then, has separated us today, so that you alone have passed on without us?

﴿They will say: "Yes..."﴾ But your outward appearances were with us, while your inward hearts were with every atheist and every wrongdoing disbeliever. ﴿But you tempted yourselves, waited, doubted, and false hopes deceived you, until the command of Allah came, and the Deceiver deceived you concerning Allah. So today no ransom will be taken from you, nor from those who disbelieved. Your refuge is the Fire; it is your protector, and wretched is the destination.﴾ [al-Hadid: 14-15].

**(Exhortation)**

The lovers of this world are between the slain and the captive: some of them have fulfilled their term, and some are still waiting.

O seekers of knowledge, you have written and studied. But if knowledge were to ask you about the house of action, you would have no answer, and if it were to examine you on sincerity, would you be found sincere?

**[Chapter: Being Deceived by the World]**

The greatest of creatures in delusion is the one who is deceived by this world, hastens toward it, prefers it over the Hereafter, and is content with it in place of the Hereafter. Some of these people say: "The world is cash, and the Hereafter is credit, and cash is better than credit."

Some of them say: "A grain in hand is better than a pearl promised."

Another of them says: "The pleasures of this world are certain, and the pleasures of the Hereafter are doubtful, and I will not abandon certainty for doubt."

This is among the greatest of Satan's deceptions and his embellishment. Even dumb animals are wiser than these people. When an animal fears harm from something, it will not approach it even if it is beaten, whereas one of these people will approach that which will destroy him, while he is torn between one who believes and one who denies.

So if such a person believes in Allah, His Messenger, the meeting with Him, and the recompense, he is among the people most afflicted with regret, because he advanced knowingly. And if he does not believe in Allah and His Messenger, then his fate is even worse.

As for the statement of this speaker, "Cash is better than credit": his answer is that if cash and credit are equal, then cash is better; but if they differ, and the credit is greater and more excellent, then the credit is better. So how much more so when the entire world, from its beginning to its end, is like a single breath compared with the breaths of the Hereafter?

As in the Musnad of Ahmad and at-Tirmidhi, from the hadith of al-Mustawrid ibn Shaddad, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The world, compared with the Hereafter, is no more than when one of you dips his finger into the sea, and then looks to see what it brings back."

Therefore, preferring this cash over this credit is among the greatest losses and the most shameful ignorance. If this is the proportion of the whole world compared with the Hereafter, then what is the length of a human life compared with the Hereafter? Which is more fitting for an intelligent person: to prefer the immediate in this brief span and forfeit the lasting good of the Hereafter, or to leave something small, trivial, and soon to end, in order to take what has no value or worth, no limit to its number, and no end to its duration?

As for the statement of the other, "I will not abandon the certain for the doubtful," it is said to him: Either you are in doubt about the promise and threat of Allah, and the truthfulness of His Messengers, or you are certain of these. If you are certain, then you have abandoned only a fleeting grain that is cut off and will vanish soon, because what is certain has no doubt in it and no cessation.

And if you are in doubt, then return to the signs of the Lord, the Exalted, which indicate His existence, His power, His will, His oneness, and the truthfulness of His Messengers in what they reported from Allah. Free yourself, and stand before Allah, either reflecting or debating, until it becomes clear to you that what the Messengers brought from Allah is the truth about which there is no doubt, and that the Creator of this world and the Lord of the heavens and the earth is exalted, sanctified, and far removed from anything contrary to what His Messengers reported about Him. Whoever attributes to Him anything other than that has insulted Him, denied Him, and rejected His lordship and sovereignty.

For it is an impossibility that every person of sound nature would reject: that the true King should be incapable or ignorant, knowing nothing, not hearing, not seeing, not speaking, not commanding or forbidding, not rewarding or punishing, not granting honour to whom He wills or humbling whom He wills, not sending His Messengers to the far reaches and regions of His kingdom, and not caring for the condition of His subjects, but leaving them neglected and aimless. This would discredit the sovereignty of even the ordinary kings of mankind and would not befit them. So how could it be permissible to attribute such a state to the true, manifest King?

When a person reflects on his own condition from the beginning of his existence as a drop of semen until the time of his maturity and full formation, it becomes clear to him that the One who has given him this care, brought him to these states, and transformed him through these stages, would not fittingly leave him neglected and aimless, not commanding him, not forbidding him, not informing him of his rights over Him, and not rewarding or punishing him. And if the servant reflected with true reflection, then everything he sees and everything he does not see would be evidence for him of tawhid (the affirmation of Allah's oneness), prophethood (nubuwwah), and the ma'ad (the Return), and that the Qur'an is His speech. We have already mentioned the manner of inference from this in the book (Ayman al-Qur'an) at His saying: ﴿So I swear by what you see and what you do not see, that this is indeed the word of a noble Messenger﴾ [al-Haqqah: 38–40].

We have also mentioned a portion of this at His saying: ﴿And within yourselves; will you not see?﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 21].

And that the human being is himself evidence for the existence of his Creator, His oneness, the truthfulness of His Messengers, and the affirmation of His attributes of perfection.

It is therefore clear that the one who neglects is deceived in either case: whether he affirms and is certain, or he denies and is in doubt.

How can certainty about the Return coexist with neglect of action?

If you say: How can firm affirmation, with no doubt, of the Return, Paradise, and Hell coexist with neglect of action? Is it in human nature that a servant knows he will be summoned tomorrow before some king, to be punished with the most severe punishment or to be honoured with the most complete honour, and yet spends the night heedless and unaware, not remembering his standing before the king, not preparing for it, and not taking his readiness?

It is said: By the life of Allah, this is a valid question that applies to most of this creation. The combination of these two matters is among the most astonishing things, and this neglect has several causes:

The first: weakness of knowledge and deficiency of certainty. Whoever thinks that knowledge does not vary in degree has uttered among the most corrupt and invalid statements.

Abraham the Friend (al-Khalil) asked his Lord to show him the giving of life to the dead with his own eyes, even though he already knew of the Lord's power to do so, in order that he might gain greater assurance and that what was known by inference might become witnessed.

Ahmad recorded in his Musnad from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Hearing is not like seeing."

When weakness of knowledge is joined by its absence from the mind, or its being absent from the heart for much or most of the time due to preoccupation with what opposes it; and when there is added to this the demands of nature, the dominance of desire, the rule of lust, the embellishment of the self, the deception of Satan, the slowness of the promise (in the mind's perception), long hopes, the slumber of heedlessness, love of the immediate, the ease of interpretations, and the habit of customs, then at that point only that which holds up the heavens and the earth lest they cease will hold faith. For this reason people differ in faith and action, until it reaches the smallest weight of a grain in the heart.

The sum of these causes returns to weakness of insight and patience. For this reason Allah, glorified is He, praised the people of patience and certainty, and made them leaders in religion. He said, may He be exalted: ﴿And We made from among them leaders who guided by Our command when they were patient and used to be certain of Our signs﴾ [al-Sajdah: 24].

**[Chapter: The Difference Between Good Opinion and Delusion]**

The difference between good opinion (husn al-zann) and delusion (ghurur) has been made clear. If good opinion leads to action, urges it, and drives toward it, then it is sound. But if it calls to idleness and immersion in sins, then it is delusion. Good opinion is hope (raja'), so whoever's hope guides him to obedience and restrains him from disobedience, his hope is sound. But whoever's idleness is called hope, and whose hope is idleness and negligence, he is the deluded one.

If a man had land from which he hoped to receive a yield that would benefit him, but he neglected it, did not sow it, did not plough it, and yet had a good opinion that it would bring him the same yield as one who ploughed, sowed, watered, and tended the land, people would consider him the most foolish of fools.

Likewise, if he had a good opinion and strong hope that a child would come to him without intercourse, or that he would become the most knowledgeable person of his time without seeking knowledge and without complete eagerness for it, and similar things.

Thus, whoever has a good opinion and strong hope of attaining the high ranks and everlasting bliss, without obedience or drawing near to Allah by carrying out His commands and avoiding His prohibitions, is in the same position. And success is from Allah.

Allah, exalted is He, has said: ﴿Indeed, those who believed and those who emigrated and strove in the way of Allah — those hope for the mercy of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 218].

So reflect on how He made their hope the carrying out of these acts of obedience.

But the deluded say: "Those who neglect, who waste the rights of Allah, who abandon His commands, who oppress His servants, and who dare to violate His prohibitions — those hope for the mercy of Allah."

The secret of the matter is this: hope and good opinion occur only together with the taking of those means which the wisdom of Allah has required in His Law, His decree, His reward, and His honour. The servant takes these means, then has a good opinion of his Lord, and hopes that He will not leave him to them alone, but will make them lead to what benefits him, and will turn aside whatever opposes them and nullify their effect.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 57, verse 16:

Since faith necessarily entails humility (khushu') and calls to it, Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should be humbled to the remembrance of Allah and what has been revealed of the truth?﴾

He calls them from the station of faith to the station of excellence (ihsan). That is to say: has the time not come for them to reach ihsan through faith? The realisation of this is through their humility before His remembrance, which He has sent down to them?

[Chapter: The Station of Humility]

Among the stations of ﴿You alone do we worship, and You alone do we ask for help﴾ is the station of humility (khushu').

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should be humbled to the remembrance of Allah and what has been revealed of the truth?﴾

Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "There were only four years between our becoming Muslim and Allah rebuking us with this verse." Ibn 'Abbas said: "Allah was slow to humble the hearts of the believers, so He rebuked them at the end of thirteen years from the revelation of the Qur'an." And Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Successful indeed are the believers, who are humble in their prayer.﴾

Khushu' in the original linguistic sense means lowering, submission, and stillness. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And voices will be hushed before the Most Merciful﴾ [Ta-Ha: 108], meaning they became still, subdued and submissive. From this is the description of the earth as khashi'a (humble), meaning dry, low, and not raised by rain and vegetation. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And among His signs is that you see the earth humbled; but when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells﴾ [Fussilat: 39].

Khushu' is the standing of the heart before the Lord with submission, subjugation, and gathering of oneself upon Him.

It is also said: khushu' is submission to the truth, and this is one of the necessary requirements of khushu'. Among its signs is that when a servant is opposed and is confronted with the truth, he receives that with acceptance and submission.

It is also said: khushu' is the extinguishing of the fires of desire, the settling of the smoke of the breasts, and the shining of the light of reverence in the heart.

Al-Junayd said: khushu' is the humbling of hearts before the Knower of the unseen.

The gnostics (al-'arifun) agreed that the seat of khushu' is the heart, and its fruit appears on the limbs, which manifest it. The Prophet ﷺ saw a man playing with his beard during prayer and said: "If this man's heart had been humble, his limbs would have been humble."

The Prophet ﷺ said: "Piety is here," and he pointed to his chest three times.

Some of the gnostics said: "The goodness of the outward conduct is the sign of the inward conduct." One of them saw a man whose shoulders and body were humble, and said: "O so-and-so, khushu' is here," and he pointed to his chest, "not here," and he pointed to his shoulders.

One of the Companions, Hudhayfa, used to say: "Beware of the khushu' of hypocrisy." It was asked of him: "And what is the khushu' of hypocrisy?" He said: "That you see the body humble while the heart is not humble."

'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, saw a man lowering his neck during prayer and said: "O owner of the neck, raise your neck! Khushu' is not in the necks; khushu' is only in the hearts."

'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, saw young men walking and affecting their gait, and said to her companions: "Who are these?" They said: "Ascetics." She said: "'Umar ibn al-Khattab, when he walked, he hastened; when he spoke, he made himself heard; when he struck, he hurt; and when he fed, he satisfied. And he was truly the ascetic."

Al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad said: "It was disliked for a man to show more khushu' than what is in his heart."

Hudhayfa, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "The first thing you lose of your religion is khushu', and the last thing you lose of your religion is prayer. How many a worshipper has no good in him! Soon you will enter the congregational mosque and see no one in it who is humble."

Sahl said: "Whoever's heart is humble, Satan does not approach him."

(Chapter)

The author of al-Manazil said:

Khushu' is the quieting of the self and the stillness of the natural disposition before one who is great or one who causes fear.

That is, the constriction of the self and disposition, which is the quieting of the powers of the self from expansiveness, toward one who holds greatness and awe in the hearts, or toward what the heart fears.

The truth is that khushu' is a meaning combining reverence, love, humility, and brokenness.

He said: It has three degrees. The first degree: humbling oneself to the command, submitting to the judgment, and lowering oneself before the gaze of the Truth.

Humbling oneself to the command is receiving it with the humility of acceptance, submission, and compliance. And the outward agreeing with the inward, along with showing weakness and need for guidance to the command before the act, and help in it during the act, and acceptance of it after the act.

As for submitting to the judgment, it may mean the religious legal judgment, so its meaning is not opposing it with opinion or desire. And it may mean submitting to the divine decree (al-qadar), which is not receiving it with resentment, dislike, or objection.

The truth is that khushu' is submission to both judgments, which is submission with lowliness and humility to the command and decree of Allah.

As for lowering oneself before the gaze of the Truth, it is the humbling and breaking of the heart and the limbs before the gaze of the Lord upon them, and His awareness of the details of what is in the heart and the limbs. This is one of the two interpretations of His words: ﴿And for him who fears the standing before his Lord there are two gardens﴾ [al-Rahman: 46],

and His words: ﴿As for him who feared the standing before his Lord and restrained the soul from desire﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 40].

This is the standing of the Lord over His servant through awareness, power, and lordship.

So his fear of this standing necessarily brings him the humility of the heart, and whenever he is more mindful of it, he is more humble. It only leaves the heart when he becomes heedless of Allah's awareness of him and His watching over him.

The second interpretation: it is the servant's standing before his Lord at the time of meeting Him.

According to the first, it is of the type of the verbal noun being attributed to its doer; according to the second, which fits the verse better, it is of the type of the verbal noun being attributed to the one who causes fear. And Allah knows best.

(Chapter)

He said: The second degree: watching for the defects of the self and of the deed, seeing the favour of every person of favour over you, and breathing the breeze of annihilation (fana').

He means waiting for the appearance of the shortcomings of your self and your deed and their faults for you. This necessarily makes the heart humble, through looking at the faults of his self and deeds and their deficiencies: pride, self-admiration, showing off, weakness of sincerity, scarcity of certainty, scattering of intention, the motive not being purified from self-desire, not performing the deed in the manner that pleases your Lord, and other faults of the self and things that spoil deeds.

As for seeing the favour of every person of favour over you, it means that you observe the rights of people and fulfil them, and do not regard what they have done for you as your rights over them, so you do not seek compensation for them. For this is among the foolish and ignorant tendencies of the self. Nor do you demand your rights from them, but you acknowledge the favour of the one who has favour among them and forget your own favour.

I heard Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyya, may Allah sanctify his spirit, say: "The gnostic does not see that he has any right over anyone, nor does he witness any favour from others. For this reason he does not rebuke, does not demand, and does not strike."

As for breathing the breeze of annihilation: since annihilation is for him the ultimate goal, he made this degree like a breeze because of its subtlety, and he expressed it by "breeze" for the gentleness of its effect on the spirit and the intensity of its attachment to it. And there is no doubt that khushu' is a means leading to annihilation, the superior and the inferior alike.

(Chapter)

He said: The third degree: preserving reverence at the time of unveiling, purifying the moment from showing off to creation, and isolating the sight of favour.

As for preserving reverence at the time of unveiling, it is controlling the self with humility and brokenness against expansion and presumption, which unveiling requires. For unveiling necessarily brings expansion, and one fears from it excess (shath), if it is not accompanied by khushu' that preserves reverence.

As for purifying the moment from showing off to creation, he does not mean purifying his moment from showing off, for the people of this degree are of greater rank and higher than that.

Rather, what is meant is that he conceals his states from creation as much as he can, such as his humility, lowliness and brokenness, so that people do not see them, lest he be pleased by their awareness of them and their seeing of them, and so his moment, his heart, and his state with Allah are spoiled. How many a traveller has been cut off in this wilderness! The one protected is he whom Allah protects. Nothing is more beneficial for the sincere one than to realise poverty, need, and lowliness, and that he is nothing, and that he has not yet truly entered Islam if he claims nobility in it.

I have witnessed from Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyya, may Allah sanctify his spirit, a matter in this regard that I have not witnessed from anyone else. He would often say: "I have nothing, nor from me is anything, nor in me is anything." He often recited this verse:

"I am the beggar, and the son of a beggar, and so were my father and my grandfather."

When he was praised to his face, he would say: "By Allah, until now I renew my Islam at every moment, and I have not yet embraced Islam properly."

In the last part of his life he sent me a writing on tafsir in his own hand, and on its back were verses in his own hand, of his own composition:

"I am the poor one before the Lord of creatures; I am the destitute one in all my states.

I am a wrongdoer to my own self, and it is a wrongdoer to me; and good, if it comes to us, comes from Him.

I cannot bring benefit to myself, nor can I ward off harms from myself.

I have no master other than Him who manages me, nor an intercessor when my sins surround me,

except by the permission of the Most Merciful, our Creator, through the Intercessor, as has come in the verses.

I own nothing apart from Him, ever, nor am I a partner in even an atom's weight.

Nor is there any supporter for Him whom He may seek help from, as there is for the masters of authority.

Poverty is an attribute of my essence, constant forever, just as richness is ever an attribute of His essence.

This is the state of all creatures together, and all of them are servants to Him, coming to Him.

So whoever seeks any aim apart from his Creator is the ignorant, the wrongdoer, the polytheist, the defiant.

And all praise is due to Allah, filling the whole universe, what has been and what will yet come."

As for isolating the sight of favour: it is that you see favour and kindness only from Allah. He is the Bestower of it without any cause from you, and there is no intercessor for you who precedes Him with intercession, nor any means that you advanced by which you sought His kindness.

Isolation (tajrid) is the purifying of the witnessing of favour for its Walī, so that one does not attribute it to anyone else. Otherwise, it is in itself free from being ascribed to anything other than Him; the matter concerns isolating it in witnessing, so that the witnessing conforms to the Truth in reality. And Allah knows best.

(Section)

Charity, beneficence and giving are attributes of the Lord, the Exalted, and the most beloved of His servants to Him are those who possess these qualities, as the Prophet said:

"The creation is the dependents of Allah, so the most beloved of creation to Him is the one most beneficial to His dependents." They said: Allah, glorified is He, mentioned the categories of the fortunate and began with the charitable ones, the first of them, saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the men who give charity and the women who give charity, and who loan Allah a goodly loan, it will be multiplied for them, and they will have a noble reward. And those who have believed in Allah and His messengers - it is those who are the saints (al-siddiqun) and the martyrs, with their Lord; for them is their reward and their light.﴾

These are the categories of the fortunate, and the foremost of them are the charitable men and women.

They said: In charity there are benefits and advantages that none can enumerate except Allah.

Among them: it guards against evil deaths and repels calamity, to the extent that it repels [harm] even from the wrongdoer.

Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: They used to hold that charity repels [harm] from the oppressed man, extinguishes sin, preserves wealth, brings provision, gladdens the heart, and necessitates trust in Allah and good opinion of Him, just as stinginess is bad opinion of Allah.

It humbles the Shaytan, that is, charity; it purifies the soul and causes it to grow; it makes the servant beloved to Allah and to His creation; it covers over every fault of his, just as stinginess conceals every good deed; it increases one's lifespan; it attracts the supplications and love of people; it protects its giver from the punishment of the grave; it will be a shade for him on the Day of Resurrection; it intercedes for him with Allah; it makes the hardships of this world and the Hereafter easy for him; and it calls him to all other acts of righteousness, so they do not elude him.

Its benefits and advantages are many times that.

They said: Even if there were no benefit or beneficence in it except that it is an attribute of Allah, and He, glorified is He, loves whoever embodies the requirements of His attributes and their effects, then He loves the All-Knowing, the Generous, the Modest, the Concealing; a strong believer is more beloved to Him than a weak believer; He loves the Just, the Pardoning, the Merciful, the Grateful, the Righteous and the Noble. His attribute is self-sufficiency and generosity, and He loves the self-sufficient and generous.

They said: It suffices for the excellence of beneficence through wealth that the recompense for it is of the same kind as the deed. Whoever clothes a believer, Allah will clothe him with garments of Paradise.

Whoever feeds a hungry person, Allah will feed him from the fruits of Paradise.

Whoever gives drink to a thirsty person, Allah will give him to drink from the drink of Paradise.

Whoever frees a slave, Allah will free for every limb of his a limb of his from the Fire, even his private part for his private part.

Whoever eases [the burden of] one in difficulty, Allah will ease [his affairs] for him in this world and the Hereafter.

Whoever relieves a believer of a distress of this world, Allah will relieve him of a distress of the Day of Resurrection.

And Allah is in the aid of the servant as long as the servant is in the aid of his brother.

(Section)

Know that the most noble of creation before Allah, the Exalted, are the God-conscious (al-muttaqun) whose tongues never cease to be moist with His remembrance, for they fear Him in His commands and prohibitions, and they make remembrance their emblem.

God-consciousness necessitates for them entry into Paradise and deliverance from the Fire; this is the reward and recompense.

Remembrance necessitates for them nearness to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and closeness to Him; this is the station.

The workers for the Hereafter are of two kinds: some work for the recompense and reward, and some work for the station and rank; the latter competes with others for the means and station with Allah, Exalted is He, and hastens toward nearness to Him.

Allah, Exalted is He, mentioned both kinds in Surat al-Hadid in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the men who give charity and the women who give charity, and who loan Allah a goodly loan, it will be multiplied for them, and they will have a noble reward.﴾

These are the people of recompense and reward. Then He said: ﴿And those who have believed in Allah and His messengers - it is those who are the saints.﴾

These are the people of station and nearness. Then He said: ﴿And the martyrs, with their Lord; for them is their reward and their light.﴾

It was said: this is a continuation of the report about ﴿those who have believed in Allah and His messengers﴾.

He reports about them that they are the saints and that they are the martyrs who bear witness over the nations; then He reports about them that they have a reward, which is His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿for them is their reward and their light.﴾ So He has reported about them four matters: that they are saints, and martyrs.

This is the rank and station.

It was said: the speech is complete at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿the saints﴾.

Then He mentioned after that the condition of the martyrs, saying: ﴿And the martyrs, with their Lord; for them is their reward and their light.﴾

So He has mentioned the charitable, the people of righteousness and beneficence, and then the believers in whose hearts faith has taken firm root and who are filled with it; they are the saints, and they are the people of knowledge and action. The former are the people of righteousness and beneficence, but these are more complete in sainthood than them.

Then He mentioned the martyrs and that He, Exalted is He, provides them with their provision and their light, because when they gave up their lives for Allah, Exalted is He, Allah rewarded them for it by making them living with Him, being provided for, so their provision and light flow to them. These are the fortunate.

Then He mentioned the wretched, saying: ﴿And those who disbelieved and denied Our signs - those are the companions of Hellfire.﴾

The purpose is that He, glorified and exalted is He, mentioned the people of rewards and ranks, and these two matters are what Pharaoh promised the sorcerers if they overcame Musa, peace be upon him. They said: ﴿Indeed, for us there will surely be a reward if we are the victors." He said, "Yes, and indeed you will be among those brought near.﴾

That is, I will combine for you both reward and station with me and nearness to me.

So the workers worked for rewards, and the knowers worked for ranks, station and nearness to Allah.

The heart-deeds of these are more than the deeds of those, and the physical deeds of those may be more than the deeds of these.

(Section)

Allah's saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who have believed in Allah and His messengers - it is those who are the saints, and the martyrs, with their Lord; for them is their reward and their light.﴾

It was said: the pause is at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿they are the saints﴾, then one begins: "and the martyrs, with their Lord".

So the statement becomes two sentences: in one He reports about the believers in Allah and His messengers that they are the saints, and complete faith necessitates knowledge, action, and calling to Allah through teaching and patience upon it.

In the second He reports that the martyrs, with their Lord, have their reward and their light. The rank of the saints is above the rank of the martyrs, and for this reason He placed them before them in the two verses, here and in Surat al-Nisa'. Likewise their mention came before the martyrs in the speech of the Prophet ﷺ in his saying:

"Be steady, Uhud; upon you is only a prophet, a saint, and two martyrs."

For this reason the attribute of sainthood was an attribute of the best of creation after the prophets and messengers, Abu Bakr al-Siddiq [may Allah be pleased with him].

If there were a rank after prophethood higher than sainthood, it would have been an attribute of him, may Allah be pleased with him.

It was also said: the whole speech is one sentence, and He reports about the believers that they are the saints and the martyrs with their Lord.

On this view, the martyrs are those whom Allah calls as witnesses over the people on the Day of Resurrection, which is His saying: ﴿that you may be witnesses over the people﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143].

They are the believers, and He described them as saints in this world and as witnesses over the people on the Day of Resurrection; and "the martyrs" is then an attribute of the whole category of believing saints.

It was also said: the martyrs are those who were killed in the way of Allah. On this view, it is preferred that the speech be two sentences, and that His saying "and the martyrs" be a subject whose predicate is what follows, because not every saint is a martyr in the way of Allah.

It is also preferred by the fact that if the martyrs were included in the predicate about the believers, then His saying: ﴿for them is their reward and their light﴾ [al-Hadid: 19] would also be included in the predicate about them, and He would have reported about them three things: first, that they are the saints; second, that they are the martyrs; third, that for them is their reward and their light.

That would involve joining the second predicate to the first, then mentioning the third predicate unconnected by a conjunction. This is like saying: "Zayd is generous and knowledgeable, has wealth." The better usage in this is to make the predicates correspond, by leaving them all unconjoined or by conjoining them all, so you say: "Zayd is generous, knowledgeable, and has wealth," or "generous and knowledgeable and possessing wealth." So reflect on it.

It is also preferred by the fact that the speech becomes independent sentences in which He mentions the categories of His fortunate creatures: the saints, the martyrs, and the righteous, who are mentioned in the verse, and they are the charitable who lent Allah a goodly loan. These are three categories. Then He mentioned the messengers in His saying: ﴿We had sent Our messengers with clear proofs﴾ [al-Hadid: 25], so that includes the four categories mentioned in Surat al-Nisa'. These are the fortunate. Then He mentioned the wretched, who are of two kinds: disbelievers and hypocrites. He said: ﴿And those who disbelieved and denied Our signs - those are the companions of Hellfire﴾ [al-Hadid: 19], and the hypocrites were mentioned in His saying: ﴿On the Day the hypocrite men and hypocrite women will say to those who believed, "Wait for us that we may acquire some of your light"﴾ [al-Hadid: 13]. These are all the categories of the world. Glorified and exalted is He left out mention of the mixed-up person, who has two traits, in keeping with the Qur'an's method of mentioning the fortunate and the wretched, while mostly omitting the sincere ones, for a secret which His wisdom, glorified and exalted is He, required.

So let the person who mixes [good and bad] beware, for he has no guarantee from Allah, and he is not among the people of His unconditional promise. Nor should he despair of the mercy of Allah, for he is not among the disbelievers for whom punishment has been decreed; rather he stands between Paradise and Hell, between promise and threat, each calling him to its requirement, because he has committed its cause.

This is what those who held the intermediate position between the two positions (al-manzilah bayn al-manzilatayn) noticed, but they erred in holding him to be eternal in the Fire. Had they placed him in an intermediate position and left him to the Will of Allah, saying that he would be brought out of the Fire by his monotheism and faith, they would have been correct. But an intermediate position between two positions, whose holder is eternal in the Fire, is something that neither reason nor revelation requires; rather, the clear texts of well-established authenticity testify to the falsity of their view. And Allah knows best.

(Section)

Charity, beneficence and giving are attributes of the Lord, the Exalted, and the most beloved of His servants to Him are those who possess these qualities, as the Prophet said:

"The creation is the dependents of Allah, so the most beloved of creation to Him is the one most beneficial to His dependents." They said: Allah, glorified is He, mentioned the categories of the fortunate and began with the charitable ones, the first of them, saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the men who give charity and the women who give charity, and who loan Allah a goodly loan, it will be multiplied for them, and they will have a noble reward. And those who have believed in Allah and His messengers - it is those who are the saints (al-siddiqun) and the martyrs, with their Lord; for them is their reward and their light.﴾

These are the categories of the fortunate, and the foremost of them are the charitable men and women.

They said: In charity there are benefits and advantages that none can enumerate except Allah.

Among them: it guards against evil deaths and repels calamity, to the extent that it repels [harm] even from the wrongdoer.

Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: They used to hold that charity repels [harm] from the oppressed man, extinguishes sin, preserves wealth, brings provision, gladdens the heart, and necessitates trust in Allah and good opinion of Him, just as stinginess is bad opinion of Allah.

It humbles the Shaytan, that is, charity; it purifies the soul and causes it to grow; it makes the servant beloved to Allah and to His creation; it covers over every fault of his, just as stinginess conceals every good deed; it increases one's lifespan; it attracts the supplications and love of people; it protects its giver from the punishment of the grave; it will be a shade for him on the Day of Resurrection; it intercedes for him with Allah; it makes the hardships of this world and the Hereafter easy for him; and it calls him to all other acts of righteousness, so they do not elude him.

Its benefits and advantages are many times that.

They said: Even if there were no benefit or beneficence in it except that it is an attribute of Allah, and He, glorified is He, loves whoever embodies the requirements of His attributes and their effects, then He loves the All-Knowing, the Generous, the Modest, the Concealing; a strong believer is more beloved to Him than a weak believer; He loves the Just, the Pardoning, the Merciful, the Grateful, the Righteous and the Noble. His attribute is self-sufficiency and generosity, and He loves the self-sufficient and generous.

They said: It suffices for the excellence of beneficence through wealth that the recompense for it is of the same kind as the deed. Whoever clothes a believer, Allah will clothe him with garments of Paradise.

Whoever feeds a hungry person, Allah will feed him from the fruits of Paradise.

Whoever gives drink to a thirsty person, Allah will give him to drink from the drink of Paradise.

Whoever frees a slave, Allah will free for every limb of his a limb of his from the Fire, even his private part for his private part.

Whoever eases [the burden of] one in difficulty, Allah will ease [his affairs] for him in this world and the Hereafter.

Whoever relieves a believer of a distress of this world, Allah will relieve him of a distress of the Day of Resurrection.

And Allah is in the aid of the servant as long as the servant is in the aid of his brother.

(Section)

Know that the most noble of creation before Allah, the Exalted, are the God-conscious (al-muttaqun) whose tongues never cease to be moist with His remembrance, for they fear Him in His commands and prohibitions, and they make remembrance their emblem.

God-consciousness necessitates for them entry into Paradise and deliverance from the Fire; this is the reward and recompense.

Remembrance necessitates for them nearness to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and closeness to Him; this is the station.

The workers for the Hereafter are of two kinds: some work for the recompense and reward, and some work for the station and rank; the latter competes with others for the means and station with Allah, Exalted is He, and hastens toward nearness to Him.

Allah, Exalted is He, mentioned both kinds in Surat al-Hadid in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the men who give charity and the women who give charity, and who loan Allah a goodly loan, it will be multiplied for them, and they will have a noble reward.﴾

These are the people of recompense and reward. Then He said: ﴿And those who have believed in Allah and His messengers - it is those who are the saints.﴾

These are the people of station and nearness. Then He said: ﴿And the martyrs, with their Lord; for them is their reward and their light.﴾

It was said: this is a continuation of the report about ﴿those who have believed in Allah and His messengers﴾.

He reports about them that they are the saints and that they are the martyrs who bear witness over the nations; then He reports about them that they have a reward, which is His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿for them is their reward and their light.﴾ So He has reported about them four matters: that they are saints, and martyrs.

This is the rank and station.

It was said: the speech is complete at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿the saints﴾.

Then He mentioned after that the condition of the martyrs, saying: ﴿And the martyrs, with their Lord; for them is their reward and their light.﴾

So He has mentioned the charitable, the people of righteousness and beneficence, and then the believers in whose hearts faith has taken firm root and who are filled with it; they are the saints, and they are the people of knowledge and action. The former are the people of righteousness and beneficence, but these are more complete in sainthood than them.

Then He mentioned the martyrs and that He, Exalted is He, provides them with their provision and their light, because when they gave up their lives for Allah, Exalted is He, Allah rewarded them for it by making them living with Him, being provided for, so their provision and light flow to them. These are the fortunate.

Then He mentioned the wretched, saying: ﴿And those who disbelieved and denied Our signs - those are the companions of Hellfire.﴾

The purpose is that He, glorified and exalted is He, mentioned the people of rewards and ranks, and these two matters are what Pharaoh promised the sorcerers if they overcame Musa, peace be upon him. They said: ﴿Indeed, for us there will surely be a reward if we are the victors." He said, "Yes, and indeed you will be among those brought near.﴾

That is, I will combine for you both reward and station with me and nearness to me.

So the workers worked for rewards, and the knowers worked for ranks, station and nearness to Allah.

The heart-deeds of these are more than the deeds of those, and the physical deeds of those may be more than the deeds of these.

(Section)

Allah's saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who have believed in Allah and His messengers - it is those who are the saints, and the martyrs, with their Lord; for them is their reward and their light.﴾

It was said: the pause is at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿they are the saints﴾, then one begins: "and the martyrs, with their Lord".

So the statement becomes two sentences: in one He reports about the believers in Allah and His messengers that they are the saints, and complete faith necessitates knowledge, action, and calling to Allah through teaching and patience upon it.

In the second He reports that the martyrs, with their Lord, have their reward and their light. The rank of the saints is above the rank of the martyrs, and for this reason He placed them before them in the two verses, here and in Surat al-Nisa'. Likewise their mention came before the martyrs in the speech of the Prophet ﷺ in his saying:

"Be steady, Uhud; upon you is only a prophet, a saint, and two martyrs."

For this reason the attribute of sainthood was an attribute of the best of creation after the prophets and messengers, Abu Bakr al-Siddiq [may Allah be pleased with him].

If there were a rank after prophethood higher than sainthood, it would have been an attribute of him, may Allah be pleased with him.

It was also said: the whole speech is one sentence, and He reports about the believers that they are the saints and the martyrs with their Lord.

On this view, the martyrs are those whom Allah calls as witnesses over the people on the Day of Resurrection, which is His saying: ﴿that you may be witnesses over the people﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143].

They are the believers, and He described them as saints in this world and as witnesses over the people on the Day of Resurrection; and "the martyrs" is then an attribute of the whole category of believing saints.

It was also said: the martyrs are those who were killed in the way of Allah. On this view, it is preferred that the speech be two sentences, and that His saying "and the martyrs" be a subject whose predicate is what follows, because not every saint is a martyr in the way of Allah.

It is also preferred by the fact that if the martyrs were included in the predicate about the believers, then His saying: ﴿for them is their reward and their light﴾ [al-Hadid: 19] would also be included in the predicate about them, and He would have reported about them three things: first, that they are the saints; second, that they are the martyrs; third, that for them is their reward and their light.

That would involve joining the second predicate to the first, then mentioning the third predicate unconnected by a conjunction. This is like saying: "Zayd is generous and knowledgeable, has wealth." The better usage in this is to make the predicates correspond, by leaving them all unconjoined or by conjoining them all, so you say: "Zayd is generous, knowledgeable, and has wealth," or "generous and knowledgeable and possessing wealth." So reflect on it.

It is also preferred by the fact that the speech becomes independent sentences in which He mentions the categories of His fortunate creatures: the saints, the martyrs, and the righteous, who are mentioned in the verse, and they are the charitable who lent Allah a goodly loan. These are three categories. Then He mentioned the messengers in His saying: ﴿We had sent Our messengers with clear proofs﴾ [al-Hadid: 25], so that includes the four categories mentioned in Surat al-Nisa'. These are the fortunate. Then He mentioned the wretched, who are of two kinds: disbelievers and hypocrites. He said: ﴿And those who disbelieved and denied Our signs - those are the companions of Hellfire﴾ [al-Hadid: 19], and the hypocrites were mentioned in His saying: ﴿On the Day the hypocrite men and hypocrite women will say to those who believed, "Wait for us that we may acquire some of your light"﴾ [al-Hadid: 13]. These are all the categories of the world. Glorified and exalted is He left out mention of the mixed-up person, who has two traits, in keeping with the Qur'an's method of mentioning the fortunate and the wretched, while mostly omitting the sincere ones, for a secret which His wisdom, glorified and exalted is He, required.

So let the person who mixes [good and bad] beware, for he has no guarantee from Allah, and he is not among the people of His unconditional promise. Nor should he despair of the mercy of Allah, for he is not among the disbelievers for whom punishment has been decreed; rather he stands between Paradise and Hell, between promise and threat, each calling him to its requirement, because he has committed its cause.

This is what those who held the intermediate position between the two positions (al-manzilah bayn al-manzilatayn) noticed, but they erred in holding him to be eternal in the Fire. Had they placed him in an intermediate position and left him to the Will of Allah, saying that he would be brought out of the Fire by his monotheism and faith, they would have been correct. But an intermediate position between two positions, whose holder is eternal in the Fire, is something that neither reason nor revelation requires; rather, the clear texts of well-established authenticity testify to the falsity of their view. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 57, verse 20:

Thus He, glorified is He, informs of the reality of this world by that which He has made visible to people of insight: that it is play (la'ib) and diversion (lahw), with which souls amuse themselves and bodies are occupied, and play and diversion have no reality. They are a preoccupation for the soul and a waste of time, by which the ignorant cut themselves off, so that it passes away in vain, for nothing. Then He informs that it is an adornment (zina), adorned to the eyes and to the souls, so the eyes and souls are captivated by it through approval and love.
