Had the hearts truly come into contact with knowledge of its reality, its outcome and its destination, they would have hated it, and the Hereafter would have been preferred over it, and they would not have preferred it over the lasting, final abode, which is better and more enduring.

The Imam (al-Imam) said: Waki' narrated to us, from al-Mas'udi, from 'Amr ibn Murrah, from Ibrahim, from 'Alqamah, from 'Abd Allah (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet who said:

"What have I to do with the world? My likeness and the likeness of the world is that of a rider who stopped in the shade of a tree on a summer day, then departed and left it."

In the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi, from the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd, who said: The Messenger of Allah said: "If the world were worth the wing of a mosquito before Allah, He would not give a disbeliever a single sip of water from it." al-Tirmidhi said: this is a sahih hadith.

In Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of al-Mustawrid ibn Shaddad, who said: The Messenger of Allah said: "The likeness of this world compared to the Hereafter is nothing but that of one of you who dips his finger in the sea; let him look at what it returns with," and he pointed with the index finger.

In al-Tirmidhi, from his (al-Mustawrid's) hadith, he said:

"I was with the group who stopped with the Messenger of Allah beside a dead young goat (sakhlah). The Messenger of Allah said: 'Do you see this, how it has become worthless to its people, so that they threw it away?' They said: 'And from its worthlessness they threw it away, O Messenger of Allah.' He said: 'The world is more worthless before Allah than this is to its people.'"

Also in al-Tirmidhi, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah said: "The world is cursed, and cursed is what is in it, except the remembrance of Allah and what accompanies it, and a scholar or a student."

Both hadiths are hasan.

Imam Ahmad said: Haytham ibn Kharijah narrated to us, Isma'il ibn 'Ayyash informed us, from 'Abd Allah ibn Dinar al-Nahrani, who said: 'Isa (peace be upon him) said to the disciples (al-hawariyyun): "Truly I say to you, the sweetness of this world is the bitterness of the Hereafter, and the bitterness of this world is the sweetness of the Hereafter. The servants of Allah are not the ones who live in luxury. Truly I say to you, the worst of you in deed is the scholar who loves the world and prefers it over the Hereafter; if he could, he would make all people like him in his deed."

Ahmad also said: Yahya ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Sa'id ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz informed me, from Makhul, who said: 'Isa ibn Maryam (peace be upon him) said:

"O assembly of the disciples, which of you can build a house upon the waves of the sea?"

They said: "O Spirit of Allah, who is able to do that?"

He said: "Beware of the world, so do not take it as a place of settlement."

In the Kitab al-Zuhd of Ahmad, that 'Isa ibn Maryam (peace be upon him) used to say:

"Truly I say to you, eating bread, drinking sweet water, and sleeping on rubbish heaps with the dogs is much for one who wishes to inherit Paradise (al-firdaws)."

In the Musnad, from him (Ahmad), [a hadith]:

"Allah has struck the food of the son of Adam as a parable for the world, even if it is mixed with saffron and salted; so look at what it becomes."

(Section)

Then He, glorified and exalted is He, informs about it that some of us boast over others by it, so one seeks it in order to boast over his companion.

This is the condition of everyone who seeks something for boasting, whether wealth, rank, strength, knowledge, or asceticism. Boasting (mufakhara) is of two kinds: blameworthy and praiseworthy. The blameworthy is the boasting of the people of this world by it; the praiseworthy is that one seeks to boast in the Hereafter. This is of the same kind as the competition (munafasa) commanded, which is that a man envies another for a thing, is jealous lest it reach him without himself, and is protective of his pride over it. It is said: "nafastu 'alayhi al-shay' (I envied him the thing) yanfusuhu nafasah," when you grudge it and do not like it to reach him without you. Tanafus is a reciprocal form of this, as if each of the competitors wants to outstrip his companion to it. The reality of competition is complete desire, hastening, and racing toward a precious thing.

(Section)

Then He, exalted is He, informs about it that it multiplies in wealth and children, so each one loves to outnumber his own kind in that, and rejoices to see himself greater than others in wealth and children, and to have that said of him. This is among the greatest things that distract souls from Allah and the Last Abode, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿The mutual rivalry in piling up (wealth and children) diverts you, until you visit the graves. Nay, you will come to know. Again, nay, you will come to know.﴾

Multiplying (takathur) is in everything. So whoever is preoccupied and diverted by multiplying in any matter from Allah and the Last Abode is included in the ruling of this verse.

Among people, some are diverted by multiplying in wealth, and some are diverted by multiplying in rank or knowledge, gathering it for multiplication and boasting. This latter is worse in condition before Allah than the one who multiplies in wealth and rank, for he has made the means of the Hereafter serve the world, while the owner of wealth and rank has used the means of the world for it and multiplied by its means.

(Section)

Then He, glorified is He, informs about the outcome and reality of the world, and that it is like rain whose vegetation pleased the disbelievers (kuffar). The correct view, Allah willing, is that "the disbelievers" are the disbelievers in Allah. This is the custom of the Qur'an, where they are mentioned with this description in every place. Had He intended the farmers, He would have mentioned them by the name by which they are known, as He mentioned them in His saying "pleases the farmers (al-zurra')." He specified the disbelievers with it because they are most pleased with the world, for it is their abode in which they work and toil, so they are more pleased with its adornment and what is in it than the believers are.

Then He, exalted is He, mentioned the end of this vegetation, which is its yellowing and drying out. This is the end of the world and its destination. Even if the servant were to possess it from its beginning to its end, its final outcome is that. When the Hereafter comes, the world is transformed and turns into severe punishment, or forgiveness from Allah and goodly reward and recompense, as 'Ali ibn Abi Talib said: "The world is an abode of truthfulness for one who is truthful with it, an abode of well-being for one who understands its purity, and a place of gain for one who is safe in it. It is the mosques of the prophets of Allah, the descent place of His revelation, the prayer place of His angels, and the marketplace of His friends. In it they gained mercy and profited well-being. So who would blame it, when it has announced its sons, described itself and its people, and taken the form of its afflictions, and made longing for its joys through its delights, by way of frightening, warning and encouraging? Some people blamed it at the morning of regret, and others praised it; it reminded them so they remembered, and it admonished them so they took heed. O you who blame the world, deceived by its deception: when did it make you blame it? Or when did it deceive you? Was it through the dwellings of your fathers in the dust, or through the resting places of your mothers in affliction? How many inheritances have you seen? How many sick people have you tended with your own hands, seeking a cure for them and asking physicians to describe their condition, yet your intercession did not benefit them and your request did not help them? The world displayed to you, on the morning of his death, your own death, and his resting place your resting place. Then he turned to the graves and said: 'O people of estrangement, O people of the grave! As for the houses, they have been inhabited; as for the wealth, it has been divided; as for the wives, they have been married. This is the news of what we have, so bring us the news of what you have.' Then he turned to us and said: 'If they were permitted, they would have informed you that the best provision is piety.'"

In reality, the world is not to be blamed; rather, the blame is directed at the servant's action in it. It is a bridge or a crossing to Paradise or to Hell. But since desires, portions of pleasure, heedlessness, and turning away from Allah and the Last Abode have dominated over it, and this has become what prevails over its people and what is in it, and what prevails over its name, it has acquired the name of blame upon absolute mention. Otherwise, it is the foundation of the Hereafter and its field, from it comes the provision for Paradise, and in it souls acquired faith, knowledge of Allah, love of Him, and remembrance of Him seeking His pleasure. The best life that the people of Paradise attained in Paradise was only by what they sowed in it. It is enough as praise and virtue for the friends of Allah in it: the coolness of eyes, the joy of hearts, the delight of souls, the pleasure of spirits, and the bliss that no bliss resembles, through His remembrance, knowledge, love, worship, reliance upon Him, turning to Him, intimacy with Him, rejoicing in His nearness, humbling oneself before Him, the sweetness of intimate conversation with Him, turning to Him, and occupation with Him apart from all else. In it are His speech, His revelation, His guidance, and His spirit which He cast from His command, which He informs whomever of His servants He wills. For this reason Ibn 'Aqil and others preferred this over the bliss of Paradise.

They said: "This is Allah's right over them, and that is their portion and bliss, and His right is better than their right."

They said: "Faith and obedience are better than its recompense."

The verification is that preference cannot be validly made between two matters in two different abodes. Were it possible for them to be combined in one abode, it would be possible to seek preference.

Faith and obedience in this abode are the best of what is in it, and entering Paradise, looking upon the Face of Allah, Majestic is His Majesty, hearing His speech, and attaining His pleasure are the best of what is in the Hereafter.

So this is the best of this abode, and this is the best of the other abode.

It is not valid to say: "Which of the two is better?"

This is the best of the means, and that is the best of the ends. And success is from Allah.

[Section: The Difference Between Hastening to Good (al-Mubadara) and Haste (al-ʿAjala)]

The difference between al-mubadara (hastening to seize an opportunity) and al-ʿajala (haste) is that al-mubadara is seizing the opportunity at its proper time, and not leaving it until it has passed and then seeking it. One does not pursue matters when they have turned their back, nor before their time. Rather, when their time arrives, one hastens to them and pounces on them like a lion pouncing on its prey. Such a person is like one who hastens to pick fruit at the moment of its full ripeness and maturity.

Haste, on the other hand, is seeking to take a thing before its time. Due to his intense eagerness for it, such a person is like one who picks fruit before the time of its ripening.

So al-mubadara is a middle path between two blameworthy traits: one of them is negligence and wasting (opportunity), and the second is hurrying ahead of the time.

For this reason haste is from Satan, for it is levity, recklessness and sharpness in the servant that prevents him from deliberation, dignity and forbearance. It causes him to place things in other than their proper places, brings upon him various kinds of evil, and prevents him from various kinds of good. It is the companion of regret, for few are the ones who hasten but then regret, just as laziness is the companion of missing out and wasting.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 57, verses 22–23:

He, glory be to Him, informed that He had decreed the affliction that befalls them in their souls before He brings them into being: the souls, the calamity, the earth, or the whole of them.

And this is the best (interpretation).

Then He informed that the source of this is His power over it, that it is easy for Him, and His profound wisdom, of which is that His servants should not grieve over what has escaped them when they know that the calamity is in it by His decree and His writing. Since it was written before their creation, what has escaped them becomes easy to bear, so they do not despair over it, and they do not rejoice in what they have attained, because they know that calamity is decreed in everything upon the earth.

So how can one rejoice in a thing in which calamity has been decreed before its creation?

Since calamity includes the loss of something beloved, or fear of its loss, or the occurrence of something disliked, or fear of its occurrence, He drew attention, through grief over what has escaped, to the parting from the beloved after it has been attained, and to its loss where it has not been attained.

And by not rejoicing in it when it is found, He drew attention to preparing the soul for its departure before it occurs, and to patience with its bitterness after it occurs.

These are the types of calamities. So when the servant is certain that they are written and decreed, and that what has befallen him of them would not have missed him, and what has missed him would not have befallen him, they become easy for him, his burden is lightened, and he regards them as he regards heat and cold.

(Section)

Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi said: Ṭhanā ʿAbd al-Muʾmin, who is Ibn ʿAbd Allah, who said: We were with al-Hasan, when Yazid ibn Abi Maryam al-Sulami came to him, leaning on a staff, and said: "O Abu Saʿid, inform me about the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿No calamity befalls on the earth or in yourselves except that it is in a Record before We bring it into being﴾."

Al-Hasan said: "Yes, by Allah, indeed Allah decrees the matter in the heaven, then sets for it a term: that it will occur on such and such a day, at such and such an hour, for the elite and the common alike, so much so that a man takes up a staff, and he does not take it except by decree and destiny."

He said: "O Abu Saʿid, by Allah, I have indeed taken it, and I am free of it, yet I have no patience with it."

Al-Hasan said: "Do you not see?"

Scholars differed regarding the pronoun in His words ﴿before We bring it into being﴾.

It was said that it refers to the souls, due to their proximity to it.

It was said that it refers to the earth.

It was said that it refers to the calamity.

The correct view is that it refers to the creation (al-bariyyah) which encompasses all of this, and the context indicates it.

His words ﴿We bring it into being﴾ encompass the three possibilities in a single consistent way. And Allah knows best.

(Section)

People have greatly multiplied speech about asceticism (zuhd), and each has pointed to his own taste (dhawq) and spoken of his own state and witnessing.

Most of the expressions of the people derive from their tastes and states. Speech in the language of knowledge ('ilm) is broader than speech in the language of taste, and closer to proof and demonstration.

I heard Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah sanctify his spirit, say: "Asceticism (zuhd) is leaving what does not benefit in the Hereafter. Scrupulousness (wara') is leaving what you fear will harm you in the Hereafter."

This expression is among the best and most comprehensive of what has been said about asceticism and scrupulousness.

Sufyan al-Thawri said: "Asceticism in this world is shortness of hope. It is not eating coarse food, nor wearing wool cloaks."

Al-Junayd said: I heard Sari say: "Indeed Allah, Mighty and Majestic, strips the world from His friends, protects it from His chosen ones, and removes it from the hearts of those who love Him, because He does not approve of it for them."

And he said: Asceticism is in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿so that you do not despair over what has escaped you, nor exult over what He has given you, and Allah does not love every arrogant boaster﴾.

So the ascetic does not rejoice in the worldly things he possesses, nor grieve over what he has lost.

Yahya ibn Mu'adh said: "Asceticism produces generosity with wealth, and love produces generosity with the soul."

Ibn al-Jala' said: "Asceticism is looking at this world with the eye of its passing, so it becomes small in your eyes, and turning away from it becomes easy for you."

Ibn Khafif said: "Asceticism is finding ease in leaving possession."

He also said: "Asceticism is the heart's release from causes, and the hands' shaking off of possessions."

It was said: "It is the heart's aversion from this world without effort."

Al-Junayd said: "Asceticism is the heart's emptiness of what the hand has emptied of."

Imam Ahmad said: "Asceticism in this world is shortness of hope."

And there is another narration from him: that it is not rejoicing when it comes, nor grieving when it departs. He was asked about a man who has a thousand dinars: would he be an ascetic? He said: "Yes, on condition that he does not rejoice when it increases, nor grieve when it decreases."

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 57, verses 22–23:

He, glory be to Him, informed that He had decreed the affliction that befalls them in their souls before He brings them into being: the souls, the calamity, the earth, or the whole of them.

And this is the best (interpretation).

Then He informed that the source of this is His power over it, that it is easy for Him, and His profound wisdom, of which is that His servants should not grieve over what has escaped them when they know that the calamity is in it by His decree and His writing. Since it was written before their creation, what has escaped them becomes easy to bear, so they do not despair over it, and they do not rejoice in what they have attained, because they know that calamity is decreed in everything upon the earth.

So how can one rejoice in a thing in which calamity has been decreed before its creation?

Since calamity includes the loss of something beloved, or fear of its loss, or the occurrence of something disliked, or fear of its occurrence, He drew attention, through grief over what has escaped, to the parting from the beloved after it has been attained, and to its loss where it has not been attained.

And by not rejoicing in it when it is found, He drew attention to preparing the soul for its departure before it occurs, and to patience with its bitterness after it occurs.

These are the types of calamities. So when the servant is certain that they are written and decreed, and that what has befallen him of them would not have missed him, and what has missed him would not have befallen him, they become easy for him, his burden is lightened, and he regards them as he regards heat and cold.

(Section)

Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi said: Ṭhanā ʿAbd al-Muʾmin, who is Ibn ʿAbd Allah, who said: We were with al-Hasan, when Yazid ibn Abi Maryam al-Sulami came to him, leaning on a staff, and said: "O Abu Saʿid, inform me about the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿No calamity befalls on the earth or in yourselves except that it is in a Record before We bring it into being﴾."

Al-Hasan said: "Yes, by Allah, indeed Allah decrees the matter in the heaven, then sets for it a term: that it will occur on such and such a day, at such and such an hour, for the elite and the common alike, so much so that a man takes up a staff, and he does not take it except by decree and destiny."

He said: "O Abu Saʿid, by Allah, I have indeed taken it, and I am free of it, yet I have no patience with it."

Al-Hasan said: "Do you not see?"

Scholars differed regarding the pronoun in His words ﴿before We bring it into being﴾.

It was said that it refers to the souls, due to their proximity to it.

It was said that it refers to the earth.

It was said that it refers to the calamity.

The correct view is that it refers to the creation (al-bariyyah) which encompasses all of this, and the context indicates it.

His words ﴿We bring it into being﴾ encompass the three possibilities in a single consistent way. And Allah knows best.

(Section)

People have greatly multiplied speech about asceticism (zuhd), and each has pointed to his own taste (dhawq) and spoken of his own state and witnessing.

Most of the expressions of the people derive from their tastes and states. Speech in the language of knowledge ('ilm) is broader than speech in the language of taste, and closer to proof and demonstration.

I heard Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah sanctify his spirit, say: "Asceticism (zuhd) is leaving what does not benefit in the Hereafter. Scrupulousness (wara') is leaving what you fear will harm you in the Hereafter."

This expression is among the best and most comprehensive of what has been said about asceticism and scrupulousness.

Sufyan al-Thawri said: "Asceticism in this world is shortness of hope. It is not eating coarse food, nor wearing wool cloaks."

Al-Junayd said: I heard Sari say: "Indeed Allah, Mighty and Majestic, strips the world from His friends, protects it from His chosen ones, and removes it from the hearts of those who love Him, because He does not approve of it for them."

And he said: Asceticism is in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿so that you do not despair over what has escaped you, nor exult over what He has given you, and Allah does not love every arrogant boaster﴾.

So the ascetic does not rejoice in the worldly things he possesses, nor grieve over what he has lost.

Yahya ibn Mu'adh said: "Asceticism produces generosity with wealth, and love produces generosity with the soul."

Ibn al-Jala' said: "Asceticism is looking at this world with the eye of its passing, so it becomes small in your eyes, and turning away from it becomes easy for you."

Ibn Khafif said: "Asceticism is finding ease in leaving possession."

He also said: "Asceticism is the heart's release from causes, and the hands' shaking off of possessions."

It was said: "It is the heart's aversion from this world without effort."

Al-Junayd said: "Asceticism is the heart's emptiness of what the hand has emptied of."

Imam Ahmad said: "Asceticism in this world is shortness of hope."

And there is another narration from him: that it is not rejoicing when it comes, nor grieving when it departs. He was asked about a man who has a thousand dinars: would he be an ascetic? He said: "Yes, on condition that he does not rejoice when it increases, nor grieve when it decreases."

[Chapter: The Station of Vigilance (Ri'ayah)]

Among the stations of ﴿You alone do we worship, and You alone do we ask for help﴾ is the station of vigilance (ri'ayah).

It consists of: watching over knowledge and preserving it through action; watching over action through excellence (ihsan) and sincerity (ikhlas), and preserving it from things that corrupt it; watching over the state through conformity; and preserving it by cutting off division. Thus vigilance is safeguarding and preservation.

The levels of knowledge and action are three: transmission (riwayah), which is merely the transmitting and carrying of what is transmitted; understanding (dirayah), which is comprehending its meaning and grasping it; and vigilance (ri'ayah), which is acting in accordance with what one knows and what it requires.

So the transmitters' concern is transmission, the scholars' concern is understanding, and the knowers' ('arifun) concern is vigilance. Allah has censured those who did not observe, as they should, the monasticism (rahbaniyyah) that they chose and innovated. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We placed in the hearts of those who followed him compassion and mercy, and monasticism which they innovated; We did not prescribe it for them, but [they did it] seeking the pleasure of Allah. But they did not observe it with its proper observance﴾ [al-Hadid: 27].

"Rahbaniyyatan" is in the accusative governed by "ibtada'uha" by way of the particle of occupation (al-ishtighal). It is either governed by the very verb mentioned, according to the view of the Kufans, or by a omitted implied verb that is explained by the verb mentioned, according to the view of the Basrans; that is, "and they innovated monasticism." It is not in the accusative by virtue of the verb "ja'l" (We placed) falling upon it.

So the complete pause is at His saying "and mercy," and then one begins: ﴿and monasticism which they innovated﴾.

That is: We did not legislate it for them; rather, they innovated it on their own accord, and We did not prescribe it upon them.

Regarding the accusative of His saying ﴿except seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾ there are three possibilities.

The first: it is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), meaning: We did not prescribe it upon them except seeking the pleasure of Allah. This is invalid, for He, glorified is He, did not prescribe it upon them. How could He, when He informed that they themselves innovated it? So it is innovated, not prescribed. Also, the object of purpose must be the cause of the action of the agent mentioned with it, so that the cause and the aim are unified, as in: "I stood up out of honor (ikram)." The one standing is the one honoring, and the action of the agent that is being explained here is the writing (prescribing).

And "seeking the pleasure of Allah" is their action, not Allah's action, so it cannot be the cause of Allah's action, due to the difference of the agent.

It was said: it is a substitute (badal) for the object of "kataban-aha" (We prescribed it); that is, "We did not prescribe it upon them except seeking the pleasure of Allah."

This too is invalid, since seeking the pleasure of Allah is not identical with monasticism, so that it would be a substitute of one thing for another; nor is it a part of it, so that it would be a substitute of part for whole; nor is one of them inclusive of the other, so that it would be a substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal). And it is not a substitution by error (badal ghalat).

Rather, the correct view is that it is in the accusative as an exceptive of a disjunct (istithna' munqati'). That is: they did not do it nor innovate it except to seek the pleasure of Allah. What indicates this is His saying "they innovated it," and then He mentioned what moved them and prompted the innovation of this monasticism, which was the seeking of pleasure. Then He censured them for abandoning its observance; for whoever commits himself to Allah to something which Allah did not oblige him with of the kinds of acts of drawing near (qurab), it becomes obligatory upon him to observe and complete it. So much so that many jurists obligated whoever begins a recommended act of worship to complete it, and they made committing to it by beginning equal to committing to it by vow, as Abu Hanifa, Malik, and Ahmad in one of his two narrations (and this is a consensus, or akin to consensus) said regarding one of the two rites (nusuk).

They said: committing by beginning is stronger than committing by word. Just as he is obligated to fulfill what he committed to by vow, so he is obligated to observe what he committed to by action, by completing it.

This is not the place to exhaust this issue.

The purpose is: Allah, glorified and exalted, censured those who did not observe a drawing-near they had innovated for Allah, the way it should be observed. So how about those who do not observe a drawing-near that Allah legislated for His servants, and permitted and urged upon them?!

[Section: Degrees of Vigilance]

[The First Degree: Vigilance of Actions]

The author of "al-Manazil" said:

Vigilance is preservation through care. It has three degrees. The first degree: vigilance of actions. The second: vigilance of states. The third: vigilance of times.

As for vigilance of actions, it is perfecting them by belittling them, performing them without looking at them, and conducting them in accordance with knowledge, not for the sake of adorning oneself with them.

As for his saying "preservation through care," that is safeguarding through attentiveness, and fulfilling the right of the thing one watches over. From it comes "ra'i al-ghanam" (shepherd of sheep).

As for his saying "as for vigilance of actions, it is perfecting them by belittling them": perfecting (tawfir) means being safe from both extremes of neglect by deficiency and excess by addition, in the legislated manner regarding their limits, attributes, conditions, and times.

As for belittling them, it is considering them small in one's sight, and recognizing that what befits the greatness, majesty, and rights of Allah's servanthood is another matter, that he has not rendered Him His due, and that he is not pleased to offer his Lord his deed or any part of it.

It has been said: a sign of Allah's pleasure with a person is your turning away from yourself; and a sign of the acceptance of your deed is your belittling it, and its smallness in your heart. So much so that the knower seeks Allah's forgiveness right after his act of worship. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to seek forgiveness of Allah three times when he finished the prayer.

Allah commanded His servants to seek forgiveness after the Hajj, and praised them for seeking forgiveness at the time of the night prayer (qiyam al-layl). The Prophet (ﷺ) legislated repentance and seeking forgiveness right after purification (wudu').

Whoever witnesses what is due to his Lord and the measure of his deed, and the defect of his self, will find no alternative to seeking his Lord's forgiveness for it, and to belittling and considering it small.

As for performing them, it is fulfilling their right, making them standing (qa'imah) like an upright testimony, an upright prayer, and a tree standing firm on its trunk that does not fall.

As for his saying "without looking at them": that is, without turning to them, counting them, and mentioning them, fearing vanity (ujb) and reproach (minnah) regarding them, whereby one falls from the eye of Allah and his deed is nullified.

As for his saying "conducting them in accordance with the course of knowledge": it is that the action be in accordance with what knowledge requires, taken from the niche of prophethood (mishkat al-nubuwwah), sincerely for Allah, seeking His face, and desiring His pleasure, not in a manner of adorning oneself with them before people.

[The Second Degree: Vigilance of States]

He said: As for vigilance of states, the second degree of the degrees of vigilance, it is that he considers striving (ijtihad) to be showing off (muraah), certainty (yaqin) to be pretension (tasabbu'), and the state (hal) to be a claim (da'wa).

That is, he suspects his own self in its striving, that he has been showing off to people. So he does not become arrogant with it, nor does he rely on it, nor does he count it as a credit.

As for his considering certainty to be pretension: tasabbu' is a person's boasting of what he does not possess.

From it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The one who pretends to have what he has not been given is like one who wears two garments of falsehood."

Considering certainty to be pretension may bear two meanings:

The first: what he has attained of certainty was not by him, nor from him, nor did he earn it by exchange. Rather, it is the bounty and gift of Allah, His deposit with him, and mere favor upon him. It is a robe which his master has bestowed upon him, and the servant and his robe belong to Him and are for Him. So the servant has no share in certainty; he is only pretending to possess what belongs to Allah, His bounty and favor upon His servant.

The second meaning: that he suspects his certainty, that certainty has not been attained by him in the manner it should be, but what he has of it is like a loan, not a settled possession. So he is pretending, in his own assumption, that certainty is his property and belongs to him, when it is not so. This does not pertain to certainty alone, but to all states. Thus the truthful person considers his truthfulness to be pretension; likewise the sincere person considers his sincerity so; and likewise the scholar, suspecting his truthfulness, sincerity, and knowledge, and that his foot has not taken firm root in them, nor has a settled faculty (malakah) been attained in them. So he is like one pretending to them.

Since certainty is the spirit of deeds, their pillar, and the peak of their hump, he singled it out for mention, as a reminder of what is beneath it.

The summary is that he suspects himself regarding the attainment of certainty. If it is attained, its attainment is not by him nor from him, and he has no share in it. So he blames himself for its non-attainment, and does not praise himself when it is attained.

As for his considering the state a claim: that is, a false claim, as an accusation against his own self, a purification of it from the foolishness of claims, and a clearing of the heart from the share of Satan, for claiming is from Satan's share.

Likewise, the heart that inclines to claims is the abode of Satan. May Allah protect us from claims and from Satan.

[Section: The Third Degree: Vigilance of Times]

He said: As for vigilance of times, the third degree of the degrees of vigilance: it is that one halts at every step, then that he be absent from his presence through purity from its traces, then that he go away from witnessing the purity of his purity.

That is, he halts with the movement of his outward and inward being, to the extent of correcting it in intention, purpose, sincerity, and following, so he does not step forward hastily and heedlessly, but stops before the step until he corrects the step, then moves the foot of his resolve. When it is correct for him and he moves his foot, he separates from it. The absence from witnessing and seeing it has become sound, so he becomes absent from witnessing his advancing by himself, for his trace is himself. When he is absent from witnessing himself and his advancing by it in every step, that is precisely the purity from his trace which is himself. At that point he witnesses the bounty of his Lord.

Since the self is the place of turbidities, his separation from it was called purity. These matters require subtle perception and readiness from the servant, and that itself is a favor upon him.

As for his going away from witnessing his purity, that is, he does not keep it present in his heart, nor witness that desired purity, nor stop at it. For that is among the remnants of the self and its rulings, and it is turbidity. When he is freed from turbidity, he should not turn back to it or return to it; thus he becomes pure from the trace and becomes absent from the purity by witnessing the highest goal and the most beautiful aim.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 57, verse 28:

In His saying ﴿You will walk with it﴾ there is an indication that the conduct and movement of people which benefits them is only through the light, and that their walking without the light is of no use to them and does not benefit them; rather, its harm is greater than its benefit.

And in it: the people of the light are the people who walk among mankind, while others are the afflicted and cut off. Their hearts do not walk, nor do their states, nor their words, nor their feet toward acts of obedience. Likewise, their feet will not walk upon the Sirat (the bridge over Hell) when the feet of the people of lights walk upon it.

And in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿You will walk with it﴾ there is a wondrous subtlety, which is: they will walk upon the Sirat by their lights just as they walk by them among people in this world, whereas one who has no light cannot move one foot after another upon the Sirat, so he is unable to walk at the very time he most needs to.
